html:
The Chorotega were a people of the Pacific side of Nicaragua and the Nicoya Peninsula of Costa Rica. They spoke Mangue, an Oto-Manguean language, and their traditions say they had migrated south from Mexico some centuries before the Spanish came, perhaps around 800.

They lived in large towns ruled by councils and chiefs, grew maize, beans and cacao on the rich volcanic soils, and made fine painted pottery. Their neighbours included the Nahuatl-speaking Nicarao. In 1522 the Spanish explorer Gil González Dávila crossed their land, and in the following decades the Spanish shipped tens of thousands of people from the region as slaves to Panama and Peru. Chorotega pottery making still survives at Guaitil in Nicoya. See Nicaragua and Costa Rica.
